Thanks for the clear ask, Jamie — copying Laura for the technical details. Summary below so procurement has something concise: 

1) Metering windows and settlement: we meter committed pools at two granularities: 1-minute burst windows and hourly sustained windows. Billing for usage above commit is applied to the additional token/embedding units consumed in the hourly window.

2) Throttling policy: we offer a soft-throttle that engages when usage is consistently above the commit for >2 consecutive 1-minute windows. Soft-throttle preserves in-flight requests but reduces new allocation to keep latency SLOs for committed traffic. In practice this prevents tail latency blowups during short noisy spikes.

3) Pricing approach: we can either bill overage at a listed multiplier (example: 1.6x the committed unit price for ad-hoc overspill), or lock a capped multiplier for an introductory period (e.g., 1.2x for the first 90 days) in exchange for a 10% term-discount on the committed baseline.

4) Operational options: we can enable spillover to hosted capacity automatically for short spikes (subject to regional availability) — that option avoids throttling but is billed at the same capped multiplier unless you want a different arrangement.

Next steps: if Acme can share the 90-day forecast (thanks for sending), we’ll produce two example invoices (baseline + 20% spike day, baseline + 200% spike day) and a one-page mutual action plan. If you prefer, we can propose a 90-day pilot with a capped overage multiplier and a one-time onboarding credit to smooth the first month.

Hi Jamie — adding some technical color to Mina's note so your engineering/finance teams have concrete SLAs and behavior to evaluate. Short version: throttling is conservative and designed to protect committed traffic. Details below.

- Metering: we track kernels and token emission at the serving layer per-GPU-pool. Two rolling windows are used: 60s (burst) and 3600s (sustained). The chargeable "overspill" volume is counted from the sustained window after subtracting committed throughput.
- Soft-throttle behavior: when sustained usage is >commit for 2 consecutive minutes, soft-throttle reduces new slot allocations by a proportional fairness factor. In-flight requests continue, and we prioritize VIP/route tags (you can mark critical routes). This keeps p50/p90 stable for committed traffic while shedding non-critical requests.
- Hard throttle and fallback: if sustained overspill remains >3x commit for >10 minutes, we can either (a) engage a hard throttle (connections are queued/rejected) or (b) automatically route spillover to Redwood hosted pools if you enable spillover. We prefer hosted spillover for short incidents to avoid customer-visible rejections.
- Impact to latency guarantees: soft-throttle preserves latency SLO on committed slices; hosted spillover has slightly higher tail latency but avoids request rejection.

Operational recommendation: for onboarding we typically set a 90-day transitional overage cap (1.2x multiplier) plus a one-time onboarding credit to absorb first-week spikes. After the transition, revert to standard multiplier (1.6x) unless you choose a longer contracted cap.

Attached is a short diagram and a sample invoice calc I ran against your 90-day forecast (see drive link Mina shared). Happy to walk through in a 30-min call.
